- code/weights: GitHub link stated (https://github.com/thu-nics/AKV). No model weights released; the paper's own text says the serving engine is built on SGLang v0.5.20 and runs on eight A800 GPUs.

### 1. LiFT: Loop Flow Transformers (2610.05538)
- what: Trains a looped DiT core with per-loop regression targets on a straight path from a detached initial velocity estimate to the flow-matching target, so extra inference loops can be spent at test time on ImageNet 256 class-conditional generation.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no arXiv URL was fetched, the text was taken as given)
- key numbers: L/2 R10 with 10 steps and 4 loops reaches FID 13.16 at 7.40 TFLOPs versus dense L/2 at 16.94 FID and 8.07 TFLOPs (50 steps), with about 41% fewer parameters; best FID 10.95 at 8 loops versus dense XL/2 at 14.30 with 250 steps. Each operating point is a single 50k-sample run with no seed spread reported. The paper's own Table 12 shows FID differences of about 1.7–2% across grids, and its own appendix says the plateau differences were not tested for significance.
- code/weights: not stated ("Coming Soon" placeholders appear in the text; no repository or checkpoint link).
- practical: LOW
- why: The method is a training recipe for a DiT, and the reader runs no diffusion-transformer training at this scale; the only transferable component, a depth-indexed loop count chosen at inference, needs a model trained with this objective, which is not released. The comparisons use one run per setting, and the headline gain rests on a matched-training-budget argument that the paper itself says holds only approximately (about 0.2% overhead), with the B/2 case going the other way. Nothing here changes a routing or retrieval decision for him, though the "spend more loops, not parameters" finding is worth noting if he ever trains a small image or latent generator.

### 1. Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement (2610.12369)
- what: Proposes Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP), a frozen robot policy written entirely as code that tracks object and robot state in variables, developed offline by coding agents in a branch-and-accept loop, and evaluated on RoboDojo's 42 simulated bimanual tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself)
- key numbers: 70.24% overall SR on RoboDojo vs. 31.38% for the best leaderboard entry (PhysicalRSI, agent+VLA) and 27.96% for the best VLA. Memory 89.9% vs. 50.3% for the best baseline. Held-out test 74.9% vs. 76.7% validation on standard layouts, but randomized layouts drop to 52.8% test. Accepted-change threshold is a margin of about 4 episodes, which the appendix says is 1–2 noise widths.
- code/weights: not stated. The paper says the benchmark is public (RoboDojo, official client and judges), but it does not release the COAP library or the coding-agent loop.
- practical: LOW
- why: Adoption requires a simulator with RoboDojo's camera and mesh assets, a frontier coding agent (Opus 5.5 Max) running an offline loop for weeks, and hand-tuned perception that the paper itself says is tied to the public simulator config. The paper's own limitation section calls the real-robot transfer unresolved. The transferable idea (keep state in code, make the policy frozen and cheap, test changes with no-regression gates) is real, but it is an infrastructure-bound robotics method with nothing that runs on his hardware, so it sits at LOW. The headline also rests on a self-selected validation set and unreplicated single-development-run numbers, so the margin should be discounted further.

### 1. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World (2610.14224)
- what: Proposes a Propose–Probe–Compose step for editing an agent's execution harness (prompts, memory, skills, scripts, subagents, plugins) without ground-truth verifiers, with parallel/sequential recursion and a persistent "improvement harness" library that carries lessons across tasks.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched, the paper text was provided directly)
- key numbers: WorkBuddy-Bench Avg. GLM-5 under OpenCode: base 64.2 → Harness² 75.7 (+11.5, single step, k=1), with a further +3.9 at k=5. Ablation on WorkBuddy-Bench (Gemini 3.5 Flash, k=1): full 77.5 vs w/o library 74.4, w/o scoping 74.6, w/o composition 75.9, all single runs over three shuffled streams with SDs of roughly 1–3 points.
- code/weights: github.com/google-research/harness2 and harness2.github.io are stated in the paper. I did not verify that the repo exists or runs.
- practical: MEDIUM
- why: The mechanism is a plain agent-harness loop (files for skills, scripts, subagents, plugins; an always-on prompt; a library of adopted harnesses), which Muninn already resembles, so a replication is cheap to attempt. It is held back by an LLM judge with no reported agreement check, a Claude Opus editor (the paper's own baseline editor), and gains of 1–4 points that sit within the reported SDs and that the paper says rely on noisy single-run evidence. It also rests on a closed Google benchmark setup (WorkBuddy-Bench, LAB with 100 tasks) that I cannot run, so the headline numbers would not transfer as measured. The useful part to test is the rule that a library entry only counts when it is backed by a contrast, not by adoption alone.

### 1. Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems (2610.19159)
- what: Benchmark of 15 unpublished DOE-scientist follow-up directions, where agents write follow-up papers graded against scientist-written rubrics for integrity, completeness and sufficiency.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, so I rated from the supplied text)
- key numbers: 0/135 submissions valid under strict grading (G1∩G2∩G3); best strict G1 pass is GPT-6-Astra at 11/15 papers (73.33%); integrity-node pass rate of the top agent is 97.77% and direction-node pass rate is 83.62%. Judge consistency is 86.5% same overall grade for GPT-6-Astra versus 57.7% for Claude-Opus-5.5.
- code/weights: the paper says "Our code and data are publicly available" in the abstract, but gives no URL in the supplied text. Agent trajectories and a leaderboard are referenced in the header only as labels, with no links in the text.
- practical: LOW
- why: This is an evaluation benchmark for frontier agents running on HPC-scale and multi-GPU tasks, and the reader cannot test it on his hardware or with his models in weeks. The useful takeaway is the failure taxonomy (lenient self-verification, insufficient backtracking, scope reduction) and the rubric-with-integrity-gates pattern, which he could copy into Muninn's own verification steps; that is a design lesson, not an adoptable tool. The judge is GPT-6-Astra with a 4-run majority, and the Claude judge's paper-level consistency is weak, so the grading numbers themselves need caution.

### 1. Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation (2610.14162)
- what: Trains a multiscale residual VQ-VAE to turn text into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of discrete codes, then a ~100M transformer generates each level in parallel (about 12 levels, not one per token), so generation takes K≪L steps.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was fetched, so this is the paper's own text as provided)
- key numbers: LM1B Gen. PPL 93.05 at 12 NFE vs. DUO 97.30 at 128 NFE (Table 8); the 21× speedup is wall-clock on one H100 at batch 16. XSum ROUGE-L 28.0 at 8 NFE vs. AURORA-LM 26.6 at 128 NFE (Table 2). Sudoku hard 86.1% vs. FMLM+ 81.3%.
- code/weights: GitHub link https://github.com/HazyResearch/ncm is stated in the paper; I did not verify that it exists or what it contains.
- practical: LOW
- why: The core pattern (predict a coarse discrete hierarchy first, then refine in parallel) is interesting, but it needs a dedicated tokenizer plus a generator trained from scratch on 13B-token budgets, and nothing here runs on his browser or Muninn stack. The headline speedups are mostly against 128-step diffusion baselines, with several single-run comparisons and only a 12-step vs. 128-step gap on LM1B. The one transferable idea is test-time MBR over cheap candidates (+~7% ROUGE-L on XSum), which he could test with his existing `decide`-style routing, but that alone doesn't lift the rating above LOW.

### 1. TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing (2610.12242)
- what: Proposes a serving runtime (on top of SGLang) for token-level routing between small and large LLMs, using per-model subservers, a handoff-resume mechanism that keeps KV state across model switches, and a delayed-batching scheduler whose threshold comes from a DTMC throughput model.
- read: full (text supplied in the message; no URL was given for the paper itself, so I rated from the supplied text only)
- key numbers: 2.01–64.15× throughput over the "stronger baseline" across 15 algorithm–workload combos; at concurrency 4 on R2R, 244.56 vs 145.30 tok/s LLM-only and 89.62 official; ablation at N=8 shows delayed batching 1.25× (372.48 vs 296.86) and async 1.29× (296.86 vs 230.79), both measured against the authors' own SGLang baseline.
- code/weights: code at https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter (stated in abstract). Weights are not a contribution; the routing models are Qwen3 and the released R2R/CITER/Co-LLM routers.
- practical: LOW
- why: The mechanism is serving infrastructure: it needs a modified SGLang fork, multi-GPU placement with CUDA MPS, and two co-resident models. Nothing here runs on his hardware or his stack (Muninn's cheap subagents are API calls, not co-located SGLang subservers), so the design can't be adopted in weeks. The headline 64× number is against weak baselines (official CITER/Co-LLM implementations without batching) and the throughput gains are on one A100 box; the paper's own Table 6 shows the honest incremental gains are 1.3× and 1.25×. The one transferable idea is the delayed-batching threshold, which is a general batching trade-off, but he would have to be running token-level routing first to use it.
